screens.title: Message Storage and Delivery Guarantees
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on two tightly coupled problems in chat systems: how to store message history so it is fast and reliable, and how to deliver each message to recipients with an appropriate guarantee. You will learn why chat data behaves like time-series data, how partition keys and clustering keys influence retrieval speed, and which database families are a good fit for high write throughput. We'll also map out delivery guarantees — at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once — and practical trade-offs for building a production chat system. Along the way you'll see concrete strategies: using unique message IDs for de-duplication, leveraging durable queues and acknowledgements for retries, and simple client-side patterns to preserve ordering and handle offline users. A clear theme ties everything together: choose the simplest guarantee that meets user expectations and design storage that matches your access pattern. For most chat systems that means co-locating messages by conversation, ordering by timestamp, using at-least-once delivery with message IDs, and handling duplicates at the client. As you move through the lessons, pay attention to how each choice affects user experience, throughput, and operational complexity.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Overview
Message Storage & Delivery Guarantees
Why chat is time-series data and how guarantees affect correctness and UX.

This lesson covers schema patterns for storing chat history, database trade-offs, delivery models, and operational practices like acking, retries, and de-duplication. Expect concrete examples and a hands-on client de-duplication pattern later.

In this lesson
Message schema, storage patterns, and delivery guarantees.
Coming up
Queues, ACKs, ordering, and de-duplication strategy.
Activity
Implement client de-duplication using a received-message ID set.
Concept Map
Storage · Delivery · Ordering
Storage
Partition by chat_id, order by message_time for fast history reads.
Delivery
Choose at-least-once for reliability and de-duplicate on the client.
UX
ACKs and retries to update status: sent, delivered, read.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will design a message storage schema tailored to chat history access patterns, weigh trade-offs between NoSQL and relational options, and implement delivery guarantees that match user expectations. First, you'll learn to model chat as time-series data and pick partition and clustering keys to make history reads fast. Second, you'll evaluate Cassandra, MongoDB, DynamoDB, and PostgreSQL variants for throughput and query patterns so you can choose the right persistence layer for your scale. Third, you'll understand delivery guarantees — at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once — and practical patterns like durable queues, acknowledgements, retries, and client de-duplication. Finally, you'll be able to implement ordering safeguards and offline retrieval so messages appear consistently across devices. Each objective pairs a conceptual skill with a hands-on pattern you can apply when designing a real chat system. We'll validate competencies with a de-duplication activity and assessment questions that check your reasoning about partitioning and delivery guarantees.

screens.title: Messages as Time-Series Data
screens.narratorSegment: Chat messages behave like time-series data: a stream of events ordered by time within a conversation. This simple claim guides schema design. When messages are read, clients typically request the most recent messages for a specific chat, often in reverse chronological order. That means the fastest schema places all messages for one conversation together and sorts them by timestamp so a single read returns contiguous history. A common misconception is to prioritise a normalized relational model with many joins; in high-volume chat this leads to poor write scalability and slow history reads. Instead, choose a partitioning strategy where the partition key groups by conversation — a chat_id derived from participants for DMs or the group's ID for group chat — and a clustering key that orders messages by time. A concrete example: storing messages with primary key (chat_id, message_time, message_id) ensures that a query filtering on chat_id and limiting by time returns the latest entries with low latency. Why this matters: colocating a conversation avoids cross-node reads and supports high write throughput as writes target a predictable partition. Think about edge cases: messages with identical timestamps need a secondary clustering element like message_id to keep order deterministic. Reflect: how will your system behave under many simultaneous messages to the same chat, and how does the schema keep reads fast?

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Messages as Time-Series
Core Concept
Treat messages as time-series
Partition by conversation, order by time, handle same-timestamp collisions with message IDs.
Why this matters
  • Fast retrieval of recent history with a single partition read.
  • High write throughput because writes target predictable partitions.
  • Deterministic ordering when timestamp + message_id are used.
Example
A DM chat_id derived from two user IDs stores messages together so retrieving the last 50 messages is a single efficient query.
Schema highlight
CREATE TABLE messages (  chat_id UUID,  message_time TIMESTAMP,  message_id UUID,  sender_id UUID,  content TEXT,  status TEXT,  PRIMARY KEY (chat_id, message_time, message_id) ) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_time DESC);
Note: the clustering order returns newest messages first.
Common mistake
Over-normalizing across tables for small-scale joins; this can hurt write scaling and increases read complexity for recent history.
Key Takeaway
Design storage to match the most frequent access pattern: recent messages per chat.

screens.title: Cassandra Table Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the Cassandra table pattern commonly shown for chat messages. Cassandra is a wide-column store where the partition key determines node placement and clustering keys determine order inside the partition. In our messages table, chat_id is the partition key: all messages for that conversation are stored together. message_time is the clustering key and sorts rows, often descending so the newest messages are read first. A tertiary clustering key like message_id prevents collisions when two messages share a timestamp. This model yields very fast reads for a conversation because a single partition read returns contiguous rows ordered by time. A concrete example: when user A requests the last 50 messages of chat_id_123, the query reads that partition and returns the top 50 rows without scanning unrelated partitions. Users sometimes worry about hot partitions when group chats receive many writes; mitigate this by sharding large groups into multiple chat partitions or using time-based bucketing for extremely high-volume channels. Another operational detail: Cassandra provides eventual consistency by default. That means writes may reach replicas at slightly different times, but they converge. For chat, slight replica lag is usually acceptable if the system reconciles and shows consistent history shortly after. Consider whether your application needs stronger consistency; if so, you might pick a different database or tune consistency levels knowing you'll pay latency and throughput costs. What part of this design would you change if a channel receives millions of messages per day?

keyIdea.text: Partition by chat_id to co-locate conversation data; use clustering by timestamp and message_id to order and ensure uniqueness.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Cassandra Table
Key roles
  • Partition key (chat_id): groups conversation messages together.
  • Clustering key (message_time): orders messages by time inside the partition.
  • Secondary clustering (message_id): ensures uniqueness for identical timestamps.
Operational notes
Cassandra excels at high write throughput and horizontal scaling. Default eventual consistency is often acceptable for chat, but you can tune consistency levels if strict ordering or immediate visibility is required at the cost of latency.
Example
Reading last N messages for chat_id uses a single partition read, returning rows ordered by message_time DESC for efficient pagination.
Visual: partition & clustering
chat_id: chat123
message_time: 2026-01-01T12:01:02Z, message_id: id-7, content: "Hi"
message_time: 2026-01-01T11:59:00Z, message_id: id-6, content: "Hello"
message_time: 2025-12-31T23:59:59Z, message_id: id-1, content: "Happy New Year"
Common mistake
Failing to plan for very hot partitions in large group chats; consider sharding or bucketing if a single chat receives extreme write volume.
Key Takeaway

Cassandra's partition + clustering model matches chat access: store conversation data together and order by time for fast, paginated reads.

screens.title: Choosing the Right Database
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing a database for chat persistence depends on expected write throughput, query patterns, operational model, and consistency needs. Cassandra and DynamoDB are natural fits for large-scale time-series writes because they allow partition-based scaling and predictable performance for key-based lookups. MongoDB offers flexibility with documents and a powerful aggregation pipeline, and it can scale with sharding. PostgreSQL with time-series extensions like TimescaleDB can work well at smaller scales or when relational features are required. A concrete example: if you expect tens of thousands of writes per second and mostly read-by-chat_id patterns, Cassandra or DynamoDB will give the predictable write path and low-latency reads. If you need complex transactions or multi-table joins with ACID semantics, PostgreSQL could be a better match but will require careful partitioning. Important misconceptions: people sometimes prefer relational databases for familiarity, but that can lead to write bottlenecks when message volume grows. Another mistake is assuming one size fits all: you can mix technologies — for example, use a wide-column store for message history and a relational DB for user profiles and permissions. Operationally, consider backups, replication, and cost. Finally, think about consistency tuning: choosing stronger consistency increases latency, so align the database choice with the user experience you need.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Database Choices
Cassandra / DynamoDB
Designed for high write throughput, predictable partition reads, and time-series workload patterns. Best when write scale is the top priority.
MongoDB
Flexible document model and aggregation; works well with sharding. Good when you want schema flexibility and complex read pipelines.
PostgreSQL / TimescaleDB
Relational guarantees and extensions for time-series. Appropriate for smaller scale or when strong transactions matter.
Decision factors
  • Write throughput and predictable partitioning.
  • Query patterns: reads by chat_id and pagination.
  • Consistency requirements and latency budget.
  • Operational complexity and cost.
Concrete pattern
Use a wide-column store for the message timeline and a relational store for user metadata. This division reduces cross-system joins and keeps message writes efficient.
Key Takeaway

Match the database to the workload: time-series writes favour wide-column or key-value stores; relational needs favour Postgres.

screens.title: Delivery Guarantees Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Delivery guarantees define what the system promises about message delivery and are central to user expectations. At-most-once means a message is sent at most once and may be lost if there are failures; this is rarely acceptable for chat because users expect reliability. At-least-once guarantees that a message will be delivered but possibly multiple times; this is common in distributed message queues and acceptable for chat when clients can de-duplicate messages using unique message IDs. Exactly-once means the message is delivered precisely once; implementing it in distributed systems requires extra coordination, idempotent operations, or distributed transactions, and it comes with performance costs. A concrete scenario clarifies these differences: if a user sends a text and the network fails before an acknowledgement, at-most-once could drop the message; at-least-once would retry until acknowledgement so the recipient eventually sees the message but might receive duplicates; exactly-once would ensure a single arrival but requires more complex infrastructure. For chat, the pragmatic choice is often at-least-once plus client de-duplication because it balances reliability, performance, and operational complexity. A misconception worth noting is thinking exactly-once is simply a flag you flip — in practice it involves idempotent operations or transactional guarantees across systems. Ask yourself: which messages in your product truly require the extra cost of exactly-once?

keyIdea.title: Guarantee summary
keyIdea.text: At-least-once balances reliability and cost for chat; exactly-once is expensive and usually unnecessary for normal messaging.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Delivery Guarantees
At-most-once
Sent at most once; may be lost. Not suitable for reliable chat.
At-least-once
Guaranteed delivery but duplicates possible; requires de-duplication with message IDs.
Exactly-once
Delivered once with no duplicates; expensive and operationally complex in distributed systems.
Concrete example
A message is published to a queue. With at-least-once the queue retries until an ack arrives; duplicates are possible. With exactly-once you must ensure processing is idempotent or coordinated so the message is not applied twice.
Misconception
Exactly-once is not a simple configuration switch. It requires design changes like idempotency, dedup tables, or distributed transactions.
Key Takeaway

Choose at-least-once with de-duplication for chat; reserve exactly-once for critical, high-value messages only.

screens.title: At-Least-Once Delivery with Queues and ACKs
screens.narratorSegment: At-least-once delivery is achieved by using a durable message queue and requiring acknowledgements from the consumer after successful processing. The typical flow is: the sender publishes a message to a durable queue; the consumer takes the message and processes it, for example storing it in the messages table and pushing it to connected clients; once processing completes, the consumer sends an acknowledgement to the queue; if the acknowledgement never arrives, the queue will retry delivery. This flow guarantees eventual delivery but can create duplicates if the consumer processed the message but the acknowledgment was lost. To handle this, include a unique client-generated message_id with each message so the consumer or client can detect duplicates. A concrete scenario: a mobile client sends a message which the server stores, enqueues for delivery to offline recipients, and then returns a success to the sender after persistence. If the delivery queue retries, receivers may see the same message more than once unless they check the message_id. A common mistake is assuming the queue alone prevents duplicates; the system must be designed to accept duplicate deliveries gracefully using idempotent storage updates or de-duplication checks. Think through latency and back-pressure: ack-based flows can build pressure on consumers; you must design consumers to acknowledge only after durable processing completes.

keyIdea.title: Process insight
keyIdea.text: Durable queues plus consumer acknowledgements ensure messages are not lost, but you must plan for duplicates and consumer capacity.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › At-Least-Once Flow
1. Publisher
Client publishes message with a unique message_id to a durable queue.
2. Consumer
Consumer processes message: persist to messages table, notify connected recipients.
3. Acknowledgement
Consumer sends ACK; the queue removes the message. If no ACK, the queue retries delivery.
Example scenario
A sender's device publishes a message while on cellular; if the ACK doesn't reach the queue due to an outage, the queue retries and the recipient may see the message more than once unless they check message_id.
Common mistake
Acknowledging before durable processing completes. Only ACK after persistence and, if needed, downstream notifications are recorded.
Key Takeaway

Make consumers acknowledge only after durable work completes and use message IDs to guard against duplicates created by retries.

screens.title: Exactly-Once vs At-Least-Once & Idempotency
screens.narratorSegment: Exactly-once semantics guarantee a single visible side-effect for each message, but are costly. Achieving this often requires distributed transactions, deduplication tables, or idempotent operations. Idempotency means applying the same operation multiple times has the same effect as applying it once. For chat, idempotent writes can help: if storing a message is implemented as 'upsert by message_id' then repeated deliveries will not create new rows. Another pattern is a dedup table keyed by message_id where the consumer checks and sets an entry atomically before applying the message. These approaches reduce duplicates without full transactional overhead. The trade-offs are performance and complexity: deduplication tables require careful TTL and compaction policies; distributed transactions add latency and reduce throughput. For most chat scenarios exactly-once is overkill; at-least-once with message-id-based idempotency or simple upserts balances cost and correctness. A concrete example: instead of inserting blindly, store messages with message_id as the primary key or include a uniqueness constraint and ignore duplicate insert errors. Misconception: thinking idempotency eliminates retries — it doesn't prevent retries but ensures retries are harmless. Close by examining which parts of your pipeline must be idempotent: storage, notification, and read-model updates are good candidates.

keyIdea.text: Use idempotency or deduplication to get most benefits of exactly-once without the full cost; exactly-once is only for high-value cases.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › Exactly-once vs At-least-once
Idempotency pattern
Store or upsert by message_id so repeated deliveries do not create duplicate visible effects.
Deduplication table
Write an entry keyed by message_id before processing; if it already exists, skip processing. Manage retention and TTL for dedup entries.
Misconception
Idempotency does not remove the need for retries; it makes retries safe.
Concrete example
Use an upsert where message_id is unique. If a duplicate insert occurs, the operation becomes a no-op or an update instead of duplicating data.
Operational cost
Dedup tables and transactional guarantees increase storage and latency. Reserve exactly-once where business correctness demands it, otherwise rely on idempotency.
Key Takeaway

Idempotency and deduplication give you much of exactly-once's benefits with lower cost; use them as a practical compromise.

screens.title: Ordering, Offline Delivery, and Status Updates
screens.narratorSegment: Ordering is essential for readability. Use message_time as an ordering key and fall back to message_id or sequence numbers for concurrent messages that share timestamps. For offline users, messages must be persisted and made queryable so when a client reconnects it can request messages since its last known timestamp or message_id. The notification service complements storage by sending push notifications to devices to prompt them to fetch missed messages. For message status like sent, delivered, and read, design idempotent updates: a client should ACK when a message is received and the server should record that as a status change. Be careful not to rely on immediate push delivery to mark messages delivered; instead update status after the recipient client confirms receipt. A common pitfall is depending solely on delivery receipts that may be lost; design the client to periodically reconcile by querying the message store for missing updates since the last known timestamp. A concrete example: a user offline for several hours opens the app — the client requests messages since its last message_id, receives twenty messages, and then sends ACKs for those messages so the server updates status to delivered or read. Consider ordering implications when multiple devices belong to the same user; reconcile by using message_time plus device sequence metadata to present a consistent timeline. End by considering: how will you recover and reconcile divergent client timelines after a partition?

Ordering strategy
Use message_time as clustering key and message_id or a sequence number to break ties. This gives deterministic order even for concurrent sends.
Offline retrieval
Clients request messages since last message_time or message_id. Store messages durably so offline users receive missed messages on reconnect.
Status updates

Example scenario
A user offline for hours reconnects and fetches messages since their last message_id. After displaying, the client ACKs each message to update server-side delivery status.

Relying only on push notifications to mark delivery. Notifications can be dropped — use client ACKs and store status changes durably.

Persist messages and use timestamp+ID ordering; rely on client ACKs to update delivery/read status reliably.

screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks through a straightforward client-side de-duplication strategy when a server provides at-least-once delivery. The key idea is to maintain a set of received message IDs and check each incoming message against that set. If the ID is new, display the message and record the ID; if it already exists, log and ignore the duplicate. This pattern is memory-efficient for a session and can be persisted to local storage if you need cross-session durability. The provided Python pseudocode is an explicit example: the ChatClient initializes a set called received_message_ids, uses a display helper to print messages, and a logging helper for duplicates. The process_incoming_message method parses JSON, extracts message_id, verifies presence, and either displays or logs a duplicate. A practical extension is to persist recent message IDs to disk with a bounded size or TTL to prevent unbounded memory growth. A common misconception is that deduplication must be server-side; while server dedup is valuable, client-side checks are efficient and reduce user-facing duplicates. After you study the code, think about persistence: how would you persist the set across restarts, and what eviction policy would you use for older message IDs?

Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › De-duplication
What the code does
Parses incoming JSON, checks message_id against received_message_ids, displays new messages, and logs duplicates.
Production tip: persist recent IDs to local storage and evict old entries to bound memory usage.
Pro Tip

Use a time-based TTL or LRU eviction for stored IDs so the set doesn't grow without bound.

import uuid
import json
import datetime

class ChatClient:
  def __init__(self, client_id):
    self.client_id = client_id
    self.received_message_ids = set()
    print(f"ChatClient {self.client_id} initialized.")

  def _display_message(self, message):
    # Simulates displaying a message to the user.
    print(f"[{self.client_id}] DISPLAYED: {message['sender_name']} ({message['sender_id']}): {message['content']} @ {message['timestamp']}")

  def _log_duplicate(self, message_id):
    # Simulates logging a duplicate message.
    print(f"[{self.client_id}] DUPLICATE DETECTED: Message ID {message_id} already processed. Ignoring.")

  def process_incoming_message(self, message_json):
    # Processes an incoming message, handling de-duplication.
    try:
      message = json.loads(message_json)
      message_id = message.get('message_id')

      if not message_id:
        print(f"[{self.client_id}] ERROR: Message received without message_id. Cannot de-duplicate.")
        return

      if message_id in self.received_message_ids:
        self._log_duplicate(message_id)
      else:
        self.received_message_ids.add(message_id)
        self._display_message(message)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
      print(f"[{self.client_id}] ERROR: Invalid JSON message received: {message_json}")
Example usage
Instantiate ChatClient, simulate messages and duplicates; the client filters duplicates using message_id set.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on two tightly coupled problems in chat systems: how to store message history so it is fast and reliable, and how to deliver each message to recipients with an appropriate guarantee. You will learn why chat data behaves like time-series data, how partition keys and clustering keys influence retrieval speed, and which database families are a good fit for high write throughput. We'll also map out delivery guarantees — at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once — and practical trade-offs for building a production chat system. Along the way you'll see concrete strategies: using unique message IDs for de-duplication, leveraging durable queues and acknowledgements for retries, and simple client-side patterns to preserve ordering and handle offline users. A clear theme ties everything together: choose the simplest guarantee that meets user expectations and design storage that matches your access pattern. For most chat systems that means co-locating messages by conversation, ordering by timestamp, using at-least-once delivery with message IDs, and handling duplicates at the client. As you move through the lessons, pay attention to how each choice affects user experience, throughput, and operational complexity.

By the end of this chapter you will design a message storage schema tailored to chat history access patterns, weigh trade-offs between NoSQL and relational options, and implement delivery guarantees that match user expectations. First, you'll learn to model chat as time-series data and pick partition and clustering keys to make history reads fast. Second, you'll evaluate Cassandra, MongoDB, DynamoDB, and PostgreSQL variants for throughput and query patterns so you can choose the right persistence layer for your scale. Third, you'll understand delivery guarantees — at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once — and practical patterns like durable queues, acknowledgements, retries, and client de-duplication. Finally, you'll be able to implement ordering safeguards and offline retrieval so messages appear consistently across devices. Each objective pairs a conceptual skill with a hands-on pattern you can apply when designing a real chat system. We'll validate competencies with a de-duplication activity and assessment questions that check your reasoning about partitioning and delivery guarantees.

This second objectives panel explains how we'll verify your skills and what concrete takeaways you should have. You will demonstrate creating a partitioning strategy for a direct message thread and designing a query pattern that returns the latest N messages efficiently. You'll show understanding of delivery guarantees by naming appropriate guarantees for chat and arguing why at-least-once plus de-duplication is sufficient for normal chat traffic. Practically, you'll implement a client-side de-duplication routine that maintains a set of seen message IDs and ignores duplicates, and you'll explain how ACKs and durable queues support retry semantics. The assessments will include a multiple-choice question about the benefit of partitioning by chat_id and a short code exercise where your client must correctly detect and ignore duplicate messages. These steps verify both your design reasoning and your ability to implement a robust client-side safety net.

Chat messages behave like time-series data: a stream of events ordered by time within a conversation. This simple claim guides schema design. When messages are read, clients typically request the most recent messages for a specific chat, often in reverse chronological order. That means the fastest schema places all messages for one conversation together and sorts them by timestamp so a single read returns contiguous history. A common misconception is to prioritise a normalized relational model with many joins; in high-volume chat this leads to poor write scalability and slow history reads. Instead, choose a partitioning strategy where the partition key groups by conversation — a chat_id derived from participants for DMs or the group's ID for group chat — and a clustering key that orders messages by time. A concrete example: storing messages with primary key (chat_id, message_time, message_id) ensures that a query filtering on chat_id and limiting by time returns the latest entries with low latency. Why this matters: colocating a conversation avoids cross-node reads and supports high write throughput as writes target a predictable partition. Think about edge cases: messages with identical timestamps need a secondary clustering element like message_id to keep order deterministic. Reflect: how will your system behave under many simultaneous messages to the same chat, and how does the schema keep reads fast?

Let's walk through the Cassandra table pattern commonly shown for chat messages. Cassandra is a wide-column store where the partition key determines node placement and clustering keys determine order inside the partition. In our messages table, chat_id is the partition key: all messages for that conversation are stored together. message_time is the clustering key and sorts rows, often descending so the newest messages are read first. A tertiary clustering key like message_id prevents collisions when two messages share a timestamp. This model yields very fast reads for a conversation because a single partition read returns contiguous rows ordered by time. A concrete example: when user A requests the last 50 messages of chat_id_123, the query reads that partition and returns the top 50 rows without scanning unrelated partitions. Users sometimes worry about hot partitions when group chats receive many writes; mitigate this by sharding large groups into multiple chat partitions or using time-based bucketing for extremely high-volume channels. Another operational detail: Cassandra provides eventual consistency by default. That means writes may reach replicas at slightly different times, but they converge. For chat, slight replica lag is usually acceptable if the system reconciles and shows consistent history shortly after. Consider whether your application needs stronger consistency; if so, you might pick a different database or tune consistency levels knowing you'll pay latency and throughput costs. What part of this design would you change if a channel receives millions of messages per day?

Choosing a database for chat persistence depends on expected write throughput, query patterns, operational model, and consistency needs. Cassandra and DynamoDB are natural fits for large-scale time-series writes because they allow partition-based scaling and predictable performance for key-based lookups. MongoDB offers flexibility with documents and a powerful aggregation pipeline, and it can scale with sharding. PostgreSQL with time-series extensions like TimescaleDB can work well at smaller scales or when relational features are required. A concrete example: if you expect tens of thousands of writes per second and mostly read-by-chat_id patterns, Cassandra or DynamoDB will give the predictable write path and low-latency reads. If you need complex transactions or multi-table joins with ACID semantics, PostgreSQL could be a better match but will require careful partitioning. Important misconceptions: people sometimes prefer relational databases for familiarity, but that can lead to write bottlenecks when message volume grows. Another mistake is assuming one size fits all: you can mix technologies — for example, use a wide-column store for message history and a relational DB for user profiles and permissions. Operationally, consider backups, replication, and cost. Finally, think about consistency tuning: choosing stronger consistency increases latency, so align the database choice with the user experience you need.

Delivery guarantees define what the system promises about message delivery and are central to user expectations. At-most-once means a message is sent at most once and may be lost if there are failures; this is rarely acceptable for chat because users expect reliability. At-least-once guarantees that a message will be delivered but possibly multiple times; this is common in distributed message queues and acceptable for chat when clients can de-duplicate messages using unique message IDs. Exactly-once means the message is delivered precisely once; implementing it in distributed systems requires extra coordination, idempotent operations, or distributed transactions, and it comes with performance costs. A concrete scenario clarifies these differences: if a user sends a text and the network fails before an acknowledgement, at-most-once could drop the message; at-least-once would retry until acknowledgement so the recipient eventually sees the message but might receive duplicates; exactly-once would ensure a single arrival but requires more complex infrastructure. For chat, the pragmatic choice is often at-least-once plus client de-duplication because it balances reliability, performance, and operational complexity. A misconception worth noting is thinking exactly-once is simply a flag you flip — in practice it involves idempotent operations or transactional guarantees across systems. Ask yourself: which messages in your product truly require the extra cost of exactly-once?

At-least-once delivery is achieved by using a durable message queue and requiring acknowledgements from the consumer after successful processing. The typical flow is: the sender publishes a message to a durable queue; the consumer takes the message and processes it, for example storing it in the messages table and pushing it to connected clients; once processing completes, the consumer sends an acknowledgement to the queue; if the acknowledgement never arrives, the queue will retry delivery. This flow guarantees eventual delivery but can create duplicates if the consumer processed the message but the acknowledgment was lost. To handle this, include a unique client-generated message_id with each message so the consumer or client can detect duplicates. A concrete scenario: a mobile client sends a message which the server stores, enqueues for delivery to offline recipients, and then returns a success to the sender after persistence. If the delivery queue retries, receivers may see the same message more than once unless they check the message_id. A common mistake is assuming the queue alone prevents duplicates; the system must be designed to accept duplicate deliveries gracefully using idempotent storage updates or de-duplication checks. Think through latency and back-pressure: ack-based flows can build pressure on consumers; you must design consumers to acknowledge only after durable processing completes.

Exactly-once semantics guarantee a single visible side-effect for each message, but are costly. Achieving this often requires distributed transactions, deduplication tables, or idempotent operations. Idempotency means applying the same operation multiple times has the same effect as applying it once. For chat, idempotent writes can help: if storing a message is implemented as 'upsert by message_id' then repeated deliveries will not create new rows. Another pattern is a dedup table keyed by message_id where the consumer checks and sets an entry atomically before applying the message. These approaches reduce duplicates without full transactional overhead. The trade-offs are performance and complexity: deduplication tables require careful TTL and compaction policies; distributed transactions add latency and reduce throughput. For most chat scenarios exactly-once is overkill; at-least-once with message-id-based idempotency or simple upserts balances cost and correctness. A concrete example: instead of inserting blindly, store messages with message_id as the primary key or include a uniqueness constraint and ignore duplicate insert errors. Misconception: thinking idempotency eliminates retries — it doesn't prevent retries but ensures retries are harmless. Close by examining which parts of your pipeline must be idempotent: storage, notification, and read-model updates are good candidates.
